question.worked_solution:
For this integral we choose $u={x}^{3}+x$ and $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).$ Filling in the table gives the following:

| **Derivatives** | **Integrals** | **Sign** | **Same-color Products** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{3}+x$ | $\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)$ |  |  |
| $3{x}^{2}+1$ | $\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}$ | $+$ | $({x}^{3}+x)\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}$ |
| $6x$ | $-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4}$ | $-$ | $(3{x}^{2}+1)\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4}$ |
| $6$ | $-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{8}$ | $+$ | $-\frac{3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}$ |
| $0$ | $\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{16}$ | $-$ | $-\frac{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{8}$ |

We add up all the terms of the last column to get the answer for our integral. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({x}^{3}+x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =({x}^{3}+x)\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+(3{x}^{2}+1)\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{4}-\frac{3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}-\frac{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{8}+C \\  & =(2{x}^{3}-x)\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}+(6{x}^{2}-1)\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{8}+C\end{aligned}
$$
